How software engineering is changing

The Times They Are a-Changin’ indeed. Software engineering has changed drastically in the last few years, for better or for worse we are still yet to see. I am lucky enough to have been in a startup since the very first lines of code were written, and I am also lucky enough to see first-hand the changes that AI tools brought to our day-to-day work. In both cases, it is fascinating to see something evolve right in front of your eyes. It gives you perspective on how things (companies and people) move through time, and how every decision leads to something interesting in the future. The company we were and how we worked in 2020, when we just started, is a completely different thing from what it is today in 2026.

Who am I anyway?

My name is Daniel Silva and I work as a Staff Software Engineer at Coverflex. Coverflex is a Portuguese fintech startup serving multiple European markets and our main goal is to improve compensation for both employers and employees. A paragraph from the Coverflex website explains what we do better than I do:

Coverflex is a compensation management solution that brings together every part of employee compensation beyond salary. Benefits, insurance, meal allowance and discounts all rolled into one product. For companies, it’s a way to easily give people more options and value, improving employee quality of life and the company’s bottom line. For employees, it’s the opportunity to unlock more value and create a custom compensation package that anyone can spend as they choose.

As of October 2026, Coverflex has 301 employees worldwide (the vast majority are based in Europe). Of those, there are 50 people working in the Product, Engineering, Design and Data teams (or "Data and Design", there is an everlasting dispute about which one comes first in the PEDD acronym). Our product is available today in Portugal, Spain, Italy and Germany, and very soon in more European markets. It is used every day by more than 25 000 companies and 500 000 people.

I joined Coverflex in 2020 as a backend engineer, right in the middle of the COVID-19 lockdowns. Coverflex was just starting out with a couple of months of existence, and I had the incredible privilege of seeing the first lines of code being written, the first customers buying our product, and the challenges of starting from scratch and scaling into multiple countries.

Coverflex has been a remote-first company since day one. Remote-first plays a very important role in the company culture as a whole. Being remote-first "forces" us to communicate better asynchronously and trust people to do their best work at their own pace. I know the main topic of this text is AI, but as with everything, it starts with people.

People’s agency and the drive to do things

We like to say that every engineer should be a product engineer. This means that we want engineers to have the agency to think about the product they are building in collaboration with other teams. We do not want to mindlessly receive a ticket to be implemented as-is and call it a day. Who writes the issue anyway? How does it come to be? Who decides what and how it gets built?

Engineers should have the agency to do all of that. Of course, this requires, most of the time, collaboration between different people (for example, product managers and product designers thinking at a high level about the product). Engineers are always part of the process of how something comes to exist (or go away because removing features or code is as important as adding them in the first place).

Software engineering was never just about the code you write, it is so much more than that. If I had to summarise it in a single sentence, software engineering is about solving problems (or puzzles, if you want). This requires communication, discussion and thinking at different levels of abstraction to reach some kind of solution (not always the best one, because "best" is always relative and depends on a multitude of factors).

Agency and drive are probably the most important traits we look for when hiring new engineers. We did this even before AI was a thing. Coincidentally, this also makes a perfect fit for the type of engineer I believe can extract the most out of the AI tools we have today.

I usually say that using AI is a bit like going to the gym, you need to put in your reps to get good at it. You need to be proactive in keeping up with new things and improving how you interact with these tools. You also need to get a feeling for what feels right to you. For example, when a new model is released, I look at benchmarks, but I still need to test and use the model to see how it feels in my workflow. Sitting and waiting for your company or other people to tell you what to do and how to do it does not work out in the long run (like having your company tell you which text editor to use). Usually, the learnings you and your team get compound on each other when you share knowledge. Getting better at something can be, weirdly, a collaborative experience.

Experience plays a role, but there is still hope for junior engineers

Recently there has been a lot of discussion about AI "eating" the junior engineers positions, but I don’t think that is entirely the reason. The job market is not getting back to the ZIRP times in the near future, so it is natural that the market feels tougher now to get a new job. We are still feeling the effects of this change. One of the biggest victims of this was engineers with less experience.

Having years of experience allows you to make better decisions with more confidence. It also allows you to navigate problems in a more pragmatic way, leveraging the accumulated knowledge. And this actually translates to how most engineers use AI tools. Making decisions is as important as ever, and decisions keep coming with the increased speed that AI brings. But, I’ve seen first-hand engineers with less experience becoming faster, learning more things outside of their comfort zone and making more and more decisions thanks to AI. And guess what? They have a profile with high agency, drive to learn, curious, ask a lot of questions, write a lot and share ideas, … Companies need to keep hiring more junior profiles, AI is not going to replace them, but give them new tools to improve (and contribute) faster. Having a junior engineer with a different mindset, ideas and opinions, supercharged by AI, can be a huge asset that a lot of companies are missing out.

People run at different speeds

AI adoption is not a uniform thing. People "discover" how AI works at different speeds, and that is not connected to seniority either. I’ve seen examples of less experienced engineers picking up AI tools and evolving their workflows faster than more senior engineers.

Why is that the case? I have not reached any definitive conclusion but, again, the person profile seems to play a major role in this. Engineers with an "executor" mindset tend to take longer to incorporate AI tools compared to other engineers. Which, for me, sounds odd because I would think that would be the first type of engineer that would take advantage of AI to work faster. My main theory right now is that, as I said before, using AI effectively and getting better at it requires experimentation and effort to figure out what works and what doesn’t feel quite right. And sometimes, for that type of engineer, it is necessary to create more structure and guidance to make that happen.

That is why you will see teams moving at different speeds. The engineers on the bleeding edge should help create that structure and guidance for the rest of the team that still needs to walk that path. This could be live presentations, workshops, written and video guides, one-on-one sessions, …

AI is just a tool, you still need to know what you are doing

With great power comes great responsibility. AI is a great way to learn and do new things very quickly. You can jump into a completely unknown code base and start being productive in no time at all. But if you do not understand what you are doing, making decisions and being critical about them is almost impossible. Without the mental picture of the system you are working on, you are flying blind.

I have seen other people (and myself) fall for this trap. Getting out of it can be difficult because you need to set time and space aside to really understand what you are doing. There is no cheat code or quick way out. For me, the best way to fix this is, counterintuitively, to write code or documentation by hand. Just like in school, when I would write down notes with pen and paper to study for an exam, writing code or producing a technical document by hand lets the brain process information at a reasonable pace and build the mental map that is essential for anything that comes after. Doing this will make any AI usage much more efficient in the future.

Another trap that gets annoying really quickly for everyone is when you let AI "speak for you". For me, most of the time, it is pretty obvious when I am reading something generated entirely by AI. It is usually very dense, long, and hard-to-read prose that I quickly lose any interest in reading. And we see it everywhere: in pull requests comments, in RFCs, in Slack messages, … I am not completely against it, just to be clear. I see some useful use cases, if well applied. For example, some of my pull requests descriptions are generated by AI, but always under my strict guidelines that I set beforehand about what the text should contain and how it is presented. In this pull request description example, I’ve had good success by using the show-me skill and adding the following to my global AGENTS.md file:

Always use simple and concise language, either to communicate with me or when writing things down. The main goal is that we communicate in a way that should be easily understood by everyone. Follow the guidelines from ISO 24495-1 for plain language.

But even with this, the key is to read what the AI generates and see whether it makes any sense. Writing to communicate with others deserves respect for their time by being clear and easy to read.

AI at Coverflex and my personal choices

In the last few months, Claude Code has been the default choice for almost everyone on the engineering team regarding coding harnesses. But I keep experimenting and rotating between different harnesses like Codex, Pi, Amp or Opencode.

I really like Pi’s minimalist and extensible approach. Having control of my tools and being able to tinker with them is a big plus for me. But I do like trying other tools because they keep bringing new ideas all the time, and I like to get a feel for them (and eventually bring the ones that I really like to Pi myself).

Regarding skills, I try to keep it to the minimum possible. I have been enjoying Matt Pocock’s skills. They bring a sensible approach to working with AI that matches my personal workflow of thinking about a problem, deconstructing it and analysing it from multiple angles, and making a plan for what needs to happen next.

With MCP servers, I try to keep only the strictly necessary and useful ones. For my usual type of work, Linear and Datadog are the two MCP servers that I have always configured in my coding harnesses. Linear is great for writing new issues and reading context from other projects and their issues. I tend to avoid things like Notion connected through MCP because when I tried it, it was just more distraction than useful for the AI agent. The problem is not necessarily with Notion itself but with the way we organise our Notion pages. I would much rather get context from Linear issues than Notion pages because issues are more organised and link to pull requests where we can inspect more code.

Datadog is amazing and sometimes feels like a superpower. Getting insights based on real production metrics, logs and traces is really valuable to me. For example, a few weeks ago I was able to chase down some performance issues on a very critical path in our codebase, and just by asking an AI agent to look at some samples of Datadog traces and give me some hints on where the issues might be and opportunities for improvement, I quickly had a list of a few actionable things that I could work on. Without AI, this would be the type of task that would have taken easily a week or more to investigate and solve. With AI, that week turned into a couple of hours.

But, regardless of the coding harness or any other tool that you might choose, what happens around them (and because of them) is the most interesting part for me.

Monorepos are pretty useful

A few years ago, we had all our services and libraries in their own Git repositories. This was manageable when we had a few repositories to deal with. Over time, we kept creating new libraries for different domains, and repositories piled up. It was pretty common to have to open multiple pull requests on different repositories to implement a feature, do a bug fix, or even update project dependencies.

At some point, we decided that there should be a more convenient way for us to manage our codebase. We decided that a monorepo (using a “poncho project” from the Elixir world) was the right fit for our team. This meant that with a single pull request, we could deliver all the changes that we needed. This does not come free, of course. We had to deal with a more complex CI/CD process and merge queues when multiple people were trying to merge pull requests, …

This decision, even without AI in the mix, was already pretty good for us because it made the work more convenient for everybody. Accidentally, we also created the best-case scenario for AI. Since all of the relevant code and supporting files are co-located in the same directory, AI agents have no problem going through it to find the most relevant pieces for the task at hand. We found that with direct access to the code, AI has a higher chance of producing good results compared to having access only to documentation for a certain internal library or service. Documentation gets stale if not maintained carefully, but code is the source of truth right now (even when the code is wrong, it is still the source of truth).

The importance of the local development environment

For years, we neglected the experience of running the entire backend services on local machines. This happened for multiple reasons. We have access to a staging environment where every merged commit is deployed, and everyone relied on it to run the code they wrote. Also, our system relies on a couple of external providers hooked up to these pre-production environments, but not to local machines, making it hard to run specific features end-to-end. And there are a lot of moving parts that need to be configured and started to make things work. It is a fairly complex system.

I spent months without actually running any service on my machine. I used TDD to develop, and I relied on unit and integration tests to make sure I was doing the correct thing. And it was mostly fine! But fairly recently I saw this post from Thorsten Ball where he just asks for irrefutable proof that what it has done works as intended, and I got curious how well this actually works. So we invested some time (and tokens) to make sure our entire stack of backend services runs on local machines with as little effort as possible. Using mise tasks for project commands, process-compose to orchestrate all of the service processes, and Docker containers for PostgreSQL, LocalStack (to simulate some AWS services) and Grafana/Loki/Tempo (even though we use Datadog for observability, since we use OpenTelemetry, this provides a local solution compatible with Datadog), we got to a sweet spot where we could start and clean up all the services and dependencies with a single command. The remaining challenge was dealing with the external providers the services depend on. The solution is to have local simulators of those services, and you would be pretty surprised to see how effective AI agents are at creating these simulators if you point them at some documentation and the code that interacts with these providers.

Finally, after all of these years, having the option to actually run the software we get to work on every day felt really good. And things got even better when we saw the results of having AI agents using the local environment. The manual testing I was doing on the pre-production environments was now being done automatically by AI (with the help of agent-browser) to prove to me that what it just implemented works as expected. This can catch problems you only see when all the pieces click together in a real running environment. This gives me even more confidence in what I deliver than the regular TDD approach I have used for years.

Remote sandboxes and multiplayer

We all work remotely, but we get “together” frequently to discuss things. Slowly, AI agents have become part of the conversation, where one of us would open Claude Code or Codex and throw some ideas at it or ask for some research. The annoying thing is that when the discussion is over, the only option is to export the conversation and share it with other people. For a long time, we missed a coding harness that was multiplayer, allowing everyone to have access to the sessions, contribute to them and read them later.

A couple of months ago we found a solution for this problem: Amp Code. With Amp, we have shared threads that multiple people can collaborate on, and that was the main thing that drew us to try it out. But we were really surprised by how much we liked remote sandboxes (the orbs feature in Amp) and how it made our collaborative work better. With this, we can collaborate not only on the discussions leading to some code change, but also on the code change itself. It is common to have threads where two or three people are giving input to a session (asynchronously), collaborating with each other and seeing the results of the changes.

On the remote sandboxes, we also capitalise on the fact that we can run the local environment and let AI inspect and act on it. On my local machine, even if I use Git worktrees to have separate checkouts of different branches, I can only run the services for one of them because of clashes between ports and other shared resources. But on remote sandboxes, each is a separate container that is isolated from everything else, which means I can run multiple local environments, one on each different thread of work. With this, I find myself doing much more in parallel than before, and I can bring my colleagues with me on any thread I have going on.

I would say this is a game changer, and I suspect we will see a trend in this direction in the near future.

Adapting our product for non-engineering AI tools

AI adoption goes way beyond the engineering team. Pretty much every team at Coverflex uses some kind of AI tool to automate or enhance workflows. One interesting side effect is that the product that the engineering team builds needs to adapt to this new reality as well.

Let's look at a concrete example: we have a backoffice that is used by Coverflex teams to manage day-to-day operations. It handles queries for lists of records and read details about a certain company/employee/transactions for customer support, handling KYB tasks, managing schools for childcare voucher networks, managing card authorisation rules, … These are real workflows that non-engineers need to work with every single day. With AI, it brought the opportunity for people to start improving those processes, making them faster and more reliable.

Since the beginning, we’ve built our backoffice using server-side rendering, and no REST API is readily available to allow automated interaction via API calls. So, what happened? People always find solutions for their problems! Using the Claude Chrome extension, browser-based automations are now possible. I am surprised by how well this works, even if it looks a bit janky.

But we quickly noticed the side effects of this. Since the automated browser use is not very efficient at some things (for example, getting a list of transactions for the past month with a set of conditions has to go over a huge number of paginated tables), we noticed the pressure on the backoffice service started to grow. We also noticed that frequently this automated backoffice access tripped our rate-limiting rules. For AI itself, parsing HTML is not very token-efficient, especially if you are doing it all of the time, nor is it reliable because some rules might be based on element classes or IDs that can easily get changed over time, breaking existing automations.

The solution is actually pretty straightforward: build a proper REST API that exposes the functionality needed for these workflows. As a bonus, if we build a well-structured REST API, building an MCP server is easy because we can plug it into the same functionality the API exposes.

The lesson here is that we need to think more and more about non-engineering teams adopting AI tools and give them a good environment and resources to have efficient, automated AI workflows. What we build (even for internal use) needs to take into consideration whether it fits into AI tool usage and plays nice with it, because everyone wins.

Accepting contributions from non-engineers

This is a very sensitive topic nowadays. Personally, I have mixed feelings about opening the gates to non-engineers with no knowledge of our services, codebase, or engineering culture to contribute through pull requests.

The first reason I feel this way is that, at the end of the day, someone on the engineering team always needs to review pull requests. Reviewing something when there is no previous context or discussion is not an easy task. If the volume of pull requests increases, we could end up in a situation where engineers spend most of their time reviewing pull requests outside their scope, or pull requests pile up because no one dares to pick them up.

The second reason, and probably the biggest one, is ownership. Who owns that code after it gets merged? Who makes sure that it is released and everything works as expected, or that there are no hidden side effects? Necessarily, some engineering team ends up owning it. At scale, this could become a real issue.

On the bright side, I feel this is actually not a bad idea, under the right conditions. First of all, there needs to be a process in place where everyone is comfortable making new contributions. Non-engineering people should have some sort of guidelines directing them throughout the process of creating a discussion about the change they want to make and how to make it happen. Sometimes, changes are really small and require no discussion at all (for example, someone at the customer support team needs an extra information on some backoffice page). On other occasions, bigger changes might require input from product, design and/or engineering teams, and in these cases discussions should happen and a plan created. When that pull request eventually arrives for some engineer to review, it is not a surprise anymore, context around it was built and there is enough alignment to make everyone comfortable and confident in moving forward. I’ve seen this exact process happen at Coverflex, and it went pretty well, to be honest. Small changes that had a big impact on the daily lives of our non-engineering colleagues happened because of this.

The big mental toll of AI usage

The big elephant in the room. There is a cost for AI usage beyond what you (or your company) pay for tokens. I have discussed this with several people, and there is a common feeling of being more mentally exhausted at the end of the day when using AI agents.

My main theory is that context switching has always been hard and more taxing than people give it credit for. Just having your day interrupted by different meetings on your calendar is enough to create enough context switching that you physically feel the effects. Working with AI agents, after you send a prompt, there is this gap in time until we get a response back that almost instinctively leads us to open up a new session or check out another session that requires our attention, which most likely has a completely different topic from what you were working on just seconds ago.

This feels powerful and, sadly, addictive. There is this rush of dopamine from being able to juggle multiple things at the same time and getting multiple things done faster than ever before. We do not realise that, slowly, we are draining ourselves mentally. If not done carefully, I suspect this is a new fast track for burnout. I have no numbers (and it’s probably still too soon to measure), but I suspect we will see in the near future a big increase in people burning out and crashing out pretty badly.

And I fear this is not just on engineering. AI tool usage has proliferated across entire organisations, so it is a natural conclusion that this pattern of increased context switching followed by mental exhaustion will start to be felt by a large portion of people exposed to it.

Final thoughts

It seems that AI is really here to stay. It has transformed (not only) engineering for the foreseeable future. There is clearly a time before and after AI got good enough, where it now permeates every aspect of the development process.

Writing code by hand is not going away either. For most of us, it is kind of like a meditation or flow state moment that we really appreciate for what it is (Advent of Code is one of the most anticipated events of the year for a reason). Even if you are creating software in your day job, doing it by hand is still the best way to better understand and get a feel for the system you are working on. But beyond that, writing code by hand is becoming less and less cost-efficient.

I don’t think software engineering is doomed. I still think AI is a tool that requires human taste and ingenuity to make it work. We will most likely need more software engineers because more software is getting created than ever. Infinite problems in the world are waiting to be solved.

Engineers need to keep up with the times and be open to new ways of working with tools very different from the past. This has happened before: more powerful IDEs were created, high-level languages were created, and magnetic tapes replaced punched cards… We can do this again, for sure.

As Bob Dylan said, “wherever you roam, and admit that the waters around you have grown, and accept it that soon you’ll be drenched to the bone, if your time to you is worth savin’, and you better start swimmin’, or you’ll sink like a stone, for the times they are a-changin’”.

Self-hosting with Kamal and why you should do it too

Originally published on Substack. This is the original article; tools and services may have changed since publication.

Contents

  • Setup the infrastructure
  • Configure and deploy with Kamal
  • Some useful commands
  • Why you should do it too
  • Sources

Lately, I’ve been working more seriously on a personal project that I work on and off for years. It is a simple personal finance web application that we use to manage our household expenses and split the bills. I decided to finally pick it up and try to finish (for real this time). I finally reached a point where me and my girlfriend could use it and I needed to put it online somewhere.

There are a lot of good options out there where anyone can publish their web application in a very convenient way (for example, Fly.io or Render just to name two of them). I have nothing against any of these options, they are great if that is what you are looking for (I tried out Fly.io for simple things and it is pretty good). But I wanted to do my own thing and control all of my resources. I wanted the freedom of having my machines and doing whatever I wanted with them. But on the other hand, I also wanted the convenience that all of these services provide, usually through a nice CLI tool.

Enter Kamal. It is an open-source project developed by 37signals and it aims to be a simple, easy, and straightforward way to deploy web applications anywhere you only need a SSH connection and Docker. The setup is just a YAML file with some basic information on where and how to deploy things. This is all I needed!

The master plan

I have a simple Ruby on Rails application and the only dependency right is just the PostgreSQL database. The Rails project generator already creates a Dockerfile to run the application in a production environment. This is very convenient because I already wanted to run the application in a Docker container in the first place anyway.

It is also important to note that none of this is specific to a determined language or framework. As long as I have a Docker image, I can deploy it.

Again, I could use any of the existing services out there to host my database (for example Neon, DigitalOcean’s managed databases, or even AWS RDS) but I again decided that it was more interesting to self-host the database as well.

I trully belive my mantra that in personal projects your guidelines to make decisions should always be:

  1. It should be fun.

  2. It allows you learn or exercise something new or different.

Remember that with technology (and mostly life in general) there is rarely “absolutely right” or “completely wrong”. Everything is a tradeoff.

I wanted a machine for the application itself and another machine to host the database and anything else that the application might depend on (for example, Redis if needed). This way, I could only expose to the world the machine with the web application and keep the other machine (or machines) only accessible through the network subnet. I don’t actually need two different machines, I could very well just get away by using a single machine and it would work just fine. But the fun factor prevailed here.

I already have the domain I want to use registered through Cloudflare so I may use it as a proxy as well. Their free tier is very nice and gives some useful extra features (SSL termination, caching, DDoS prevention, …).

Setup the infrastructure

To get things started, I needed a cloud provider. There are a lot of good options out there. After comparing prices of different providers I ended up choosing Hetzner. Their pricing is cheap, they have the exact functionalities that I need and they have data centers in Europe.

The good thing about this whole plan is that the choice for a cloud provider ends up not being a big deal because everything is vendor agnostic and later can be moved to another cloud provider or even my hardware. This also means, that if you are following along you are free to make your own choices here and the process remains the same.

With the decision where to get the servers, how to create them? I could have gone to Hetzner’s dashboard and created everything I needed there. But again, where is the fun in that right? I didn’t need to but I decided to write some Terraform scripts and keep my infrastructure-as-code mostly because it was an opportunity to exercise my small Terraform skills and that way I could document what kind of infrastructure I have and replicate it if needed. If you are new to Terraform, I recommend looking at their tutorials using Docker.

I created a directory in my project to keep my Terraform scripts and started going at it. I decided to split the configuration into multiple files but that is just for organization purposes. Having one or multiple files is the same, as long as they are all in the same directory.

# File path: infra/main.tf

terraform {
  required_providers {
    hcloud = {
      source  = "hetznercloud/hcloud"
      version = "1.47.0"
    }

    cloudflare = {
      source  = "cloudflare/cloudflare"
      version = "4.31.0"
    }

    cloudinit = {
      source  = "hashicorp/cloudinit"
      version = "2.3.4"
    }
  }
}

I started by defining my terraform configuration block when I set the dependencies for my scripts. I just needed three dependencies

  • hcloud - used to interact with Hetzner Cloud services (servers, networks, firewall rules, …).

  • cloudflare - user to interact with Cloudflare services.

  • cloudinit - utility functions for cloud-init configurations.

If you want to keep your Terraform state elsewhere other than locally (for example with HCP Terraform), here is also the place to set those configurations.

In a separate file, I defined the variables for our Terraform script.

# File path: infra/variables.tf

variable "hcloud_token" {
  description = "Hetzner Cloud API Token"
  type        = string
  sensitive   = true
}

variable "cloudflare_api_token" {
  description = "Cloudflare API Token"
  type        = string
  sensitive   = true
}

variable "ssh_public_key" {
  description = "SSH public key"
  type        = string
}

The three variables are pretty self-explanatory. The hcloud_tokenand cloudflare_api_tokenare required by their providers to work with their APIs. The ssh_public_key variable holds the public SSH key that will be placed on the server’s authorized keys list.

The actual values for these variables are defined on their *.tfvars file. Always add this file to your .gitignore and .dockerignore files!

# File path: infra/terraform.tfvars

hcloud_token=<TOKEN>
cloudflare_api_token=<TOKEN>
ssh_public_key=<PUBLIC_SSH_KEY>

I then created a file dedicated to provider configurations and started using the previously defined variables.

# File path: infra/providers.tf

provider "hcloud" {
  token = var.hcloud_token
}

provider "cloudflare" {
  api_token = var.cloudflare_api_token
}

Next, I defined the necessary data sources on a dedicated file. Data sources load up data that exists outside of Terraform (for example, reading from a file or an HTTP request).

# File path: infra/data.tf

data "cloudflare_ip_ranges" "cloudflare" {}

data "cloudinit_config" "web" {
  gzip          = false
  base64_encode = false

  part {
    content_type = "text/cloud-config"
    content      = file("${path.module}/cloudinit/base.yml")
  }

  part {
    content_type = "text/cloud-config"
    content      = file("${path.module}/cloudinit/web.yml")
    merge_type   = "list(append)+dict(recurse_array)+str()"
  }
}

data "cloudinit_config" "accessory" {
  gzip          = false
  base64_encode = false

  part {
    content_type = "text/cloud-config"
    content      = file("${path.module}/cloudinit/base.yml")
  }

  part {
    content_type = "text/cloud-config"
    content      = file("${path.module}/cloudinit/accessory.yml")
    merge_type   = "list(append)+dict(recurse_array)+str()"
  }
}

In this file, there are three data sources defined:

  • cloudflare_ip_ranges.cloudflare - Gives us access to the list of IPv4 and IPv6 addresses from Cloudflare. These will be used when defining the firewall rules to only allow incoming connections to port 443 (HTTPS) from Cloudflare’s IP addresses (since we want to proxy requests from Cloudflare).

  • cloudinit_config.web - Loads up cloud-init configuration from a local file. This cloud-init configuration is specific for the machines running the web application.

  • cloudinit_config.accessory- Loads up cloud-init configuration from a local file. This cloud-init configuration is specific for the machines running the supporting services for the web application (for example, PostgreSQL).

For the cloud-init configuration, I defined a couple of files. A base file with common settings, a dedicated file for the web application server and another for the supporting services server.

# File path: infra/cloudinit/base.yml

timezone: Europe/Lisbon
write_files:
  - path: /etc/netplan/01-netplan.yaml
    content: |
      network:
        version: 2
        ethernets:
          eth0:
            nameservers:
              addresses:
                - 1.1.1.1
                - 1.0.0.1
    permissions: '0600'
runcmd:
  - netplan apply
  - sed -i '/PermitRootLogin/d' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
  - echo "PermitRootLogin without-password" >> /etc/ssh/sshd_config
  - sed -i '/PubkeyAuthentication/d' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
  - echo "PubkeyAuthentication yes" >> /etc/ssh/sshd_config
  - sed -i '/PasswordAuthentication/d' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
  - echo "PasswordAuthentication no" >> /etc/ssh/sshd_config
  - systemctl restart sshd
  - apt update
  - apt upgrade -y --allow-downgrades --allow-remove-essential --allow-change-held-packages
  - reboot

In the base file, I set the timezone, Cloudflare’s DNS servers, disabled root login and SSH authentication with a password, and upgraded system packages. Since this is a common action that all servers should do, it is kept in the base file.

# File path: infra/cloudinit/web.yml

write_files:
  - path: /letsencrypt/acme.json
    content: |
      {}
    permissions: '0600'

For the web application servers, I created a file used by Let’s Encrypt to issue an SSL certificate. In Cloudflare, I set the proxy to use the “Full (Strict)” SSL/TLS encryption mode. That mode sets the communication between Cloudflare and our application using HTTPS, and with “Strict” it enforces that the certificate belongs to a trusted certificate authority.

With this, I have everything in place to start creating resources in Hetzner. First, I create the firewall rules, on a dedicated file.

# File path: infra/firewall.tf

resource "hcloud_firewall" "allow_from_cloudflare" {
  name = "allow-from-cloudflare"
  rule {
    direction  = "in"
    protocol   = "icmp"
    source_ips = concat(data.cloudflare_ip_ranges.cloudflare.ipv4_cidr_blocks, data.cloudflare_ip_ranges.cloudflare.ipv6_cidr_blocks)
  }

  rule {
    direction  = "in"
    protocol   = "tcp"
    port       = "80"
    source_ips = concat(data.cloudflare_ip_ranges.cloudflare.ipv4_cidr_blocks, data.cloudflare_ip_ranges.cloudflare.ipv6_cidr_blocks)
  }

  rule {
    direction  = "in"
    protocol   = "tcp"
    port       = "443"
    source_ips = concat(data.cloudflare_ip_ranges.cloudflare.ipv4_cidr_blocks, data.cloudflare_ip_ranges.cloudflare.ipv6_cidr_blocks)
  }
}

resource "hcloud_firewall" "allow_ssh_from_home" {
  name = "allow-ssh-from-home"

  rule {
    direction  = "in"
    protocol   = "tcp"
    port       = "22"
    source_ips = ["<IPV4_ADDRESS>", "<IPV6_ADDRESS>"]
  }
}

resource "hcloud_firewall" "block_all_inbound_traffic" {
  name = "block-all-inbound-traffic"
}

Looking at this file, three different firewalls are created.

  • hcloud_firewall.allow_from_cloudflare - Firewall to allow for ICMP and TCP connections at port 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS) only for Cloudflare’s IP addresses (defined on the data sources above). I only want traffic coming in through the Cloudflare proxy.

  • hcloud_firewall.allow_ssh_from_home - Firewall to allow TCP connections on port 22 (SSH) only for my home network IP addresses. I want to block SSH connections from random people on the Internet so I only allow it from my home IP address.

  • hcloud_firewall.block_all_inbound_traffic - Firewall without any rule that can be attached to any server to block everything. If no firewall is attached to a machine, every port is open.

Finally, the only thing left is to create the network and servers.

# File path: infra/server.tf

resource "hcloud_network" "production" {
  name     = "production-network"
  ip_range = "10.0.0.0/16"
}

resource "hcloud_network_subnet" "production" {
  network_id   = hcloud_network.production.id
  type         = "cloud"
  network_zone = "eu-central"
  ip_range     = "10.0.0.0/24"
}

resource "hcloud_ssh_key" "production" {
  name       = "Production SSH Key"
  public_key = var.ssh_public_key
}

resource "hcloud_server" "production_web_1" {
  name         = "production-web-1"
  image        = "ubuntu-24.04"
  server_type  = "cax11"
  location     = "fsn1"
  ssh_keys     = [hcloud_ssh_key.production.id]
  firewall_ids = [hcloud_firewall.allow_from_cloudflare.id, hcloud_firewall.allow_ssh_from_home.id]
  user_data    = data.cloudinit_config.web.rendered

  public_net {
    ipv4_enabled = true
    ipv6_enabled = true
  }

  network {
    network_id = hcloud_network.production.id
    ip         = "10.0.0.2"
  }

  depends_on = [
    hcloud_network.production,
    hcloud_ssh_key.production,
    hcloud_firewall.allow_from_cloudflare,
    hcloud_firewall.allow_ssh_from_home
  ]
}

resource "hcloud_server" "production_accessory_1" {
  name         = "production-accessory-1"
  image        = "ubuntu-24.04"
  server_type  = "cax11"
  location     = "fsn1"
  ssh_keys     = [hcloud_ssh_key.production.id]
  firewall_ids = [hcloud_firewall.block_all_inbound_traffic.id]
  user_data    = data.cloudinit_config.accessory.rendered

  public_net {
    ipv4_enabled = true
    ipv6_enabled = true
  }

  network {
    network_id = hcloud_network.production.id
    ip         = "10.0.0.3"
  }

  depends_on = [
    hcloud_network.production,
    hcloud_ssh_key.production,
    hcloud_firewall.block_all_inbound_traffic
  ]
}

This seems like a long file at first but it just defines a couple of things.

  • hcloud_network.production - Defines a new network with the given range of IP addresses.

  • hcloud_network_subnet.production - Defines a new subnet with the given range of IP addresses under the previously defined network. There was no specific reasoning behind the chosen IP address ranges, just mimicking what the Hetzner dashboard automatically creates.

  • hcloud_ssh_key.production - Add the public SSH key previously defined in the variables.

  • hcloud_server.production_web_1 - A CAX11 machine (Arm64 architecture, 2 vCPU, 4 GB of RAM and 40 GB of disk space) with Ubuntu 24.04. Attached firewalls defined previously that limit access from Cloudflare’s IP addresses and SSH from my home network.

  • hcloud_server.production_accessory_1- A CAX11 machine (Arm64 architecture, 2 vCPU, 4 GB of RAM and 40 GB of disk space) with Ubuntu 24.04. Attached firewall defined previously that blocks every port.

And that is it! I now have a Terraform script that can spin up all the infrastructure that I need. And the cool thing about this is that if I need to add something new, it is a pretty easy process. The only step left is to run it.

terraform apply

If everything works out, the infrastructure is now ready. Using the public IP of the web application server, I can SSH into the machine. But what about the accessories server? It does not have the firewall rule to allow SSH. The web application server has network access to the accessories server because they are on the same subnet. So we can use it as a proxy in the SSH.

# File path: ~/.ssh/config

Host web-server
  HostName <WEB_APP_SERVER_IP>
  User root
  PreferredAuthentications publickey

Host accessories-server
  HostName 10.0.0.3
  User root
  PreferredAuthentications publickey
  ProxyJump web-server

With this SSH configuration on my local machine, now I can access both servers through SSH using the aliases configured in ~/.ssh/config. This is nice for two reasons: first I can use the aliases instead of writing the user and IP address of the server (more convenient, easy to memorize, and remains the same if I replace the IP addresses), second I don’t need to add an extra firewall rule to the accessories server just to SSH into it.

ssh web-server

ssh accessories-server

The only thing missing is to update the DNS records of my domain (registered in Cloudflare) to point to the web application server. For that, I create an A record pointing to the public IPv4 address and an AAAA record pointing to the public IPv6 address of the web application server. I am doing this process manually going to Hetzner’s dashboard to find the IP addresses and then going to Cloudflare’s dashboard to create the DNS records. This could be also automated using Terraform in the future.

Configure and deploy with Kamal

Getting started is pretty easy. I installed Kamal using the Ruby gem.

gem install kamal

With Kamal installed, in my project directory, I ran the initialization command.

kamal init

This command creates the config/deploy.yml file, where all the configuration regarding the deployment takes place. It also creates some sample files for hooks but, for now, I am not using those. Let’s look at each block of the file individually.

service: poupas

The service value defines the name of your application. You can set whatever name you want. It is going to be used to name the Docker containers.

image: dfilipes/poupas

The image value is the name of your Docker image. In my case, I am going to store the Docker images in Docker Hub. The free tier is enough for me because it allows one private repository. You can use whatever container registry you want (for example, DigitalOcean Container Registry or AWS ECR).

servers:
  web:
    hosts:
      - web-server
    labels:
      traefik.http.routers.poupas.rule: Host(`poupas.io`)
      traefik.http.routers.poupas_secure.entrypoints: websecure
      traefik.http.routers.poupas_secure.rule: Host(`poupas.io`)
      traefik.http.routers.poupas_secure.tls.certresolver: letsencrypt
    env:
      secret:
        - RAILS_MASTER_KEY
        - DATABASE_URL

In this block, it is defined as the deployment of the web servers in a single host (in this case I am using the SSH alias defined before, but this could just be an IP address). If you want to deploy multiple instances of your web application on different servers, you just need to add more hosts in this block. In that case, you might also need a load balance somewhere (for example, on your cloud provider, part of your infrastructure). In my case, one instance is good enough for now.

Some container labels are defined so that Traefik can issue an SSL certificate using Let’s Encrypt.

Finally, some secret environment variables are defined. You can define any environment variable that you need. The values for these environment variables are stored in a .env file in the root directory of the project (don’t forget to add this file to the .gitignore and .dockerignore files).

registry:
  username: dfilipes
  password:
    - KAMAL_REGISTRY_PASSWORD

Next, I define the username and secret environment variable for the credentials for my chosen container registry (in my case, DockerHub). The KAMAL_REGISTRY_PASSWORD value also is stored on the .env file. This should not be your account password. You should generate an access token on your container registry and use it here.

accessories:
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    host: poupas-accessories
    port: 5432
    env:
      clear:
        POSTGRES_USER: postgres
        POSTGRES_DB: postgres
      secret:
        - POSTGRES_PASSWORD
    directories:
      - data/postgres:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    files:
      - infra/postgres/postgresql.conf:/usr/local/share/postgresql/postgresql.conf.sample
      - db/production.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/setup.sql

In this block, I configure my only accessory for now, the db accessory. At this point, this should look familiar if you already have some experience with Docker. If you squint your eyes, this almost looks like a docker-compose definition. A Docker image is defined, the host is just our single accessories server (still using the SSH alias defined before), the exposed port, some environment variables required by the PostgreSQL image, the volume mount for the data directory, and some extra files used to configure PostgreSQL and initial database setup.

During my research on how to set this, I found PGTune to generate some initial configuration for PostgreSQL. You just insert some basic information about your server and your expected workload and the tool suggests a configuration.

# File path: infra/postgres/postgresql.conf

# DB Version: 16
# OS Type: linux
# DB Type: web
# Total Memory (RAM): 4 GB
# CPUs num: 2
# Data Storage: ssd

listen_addresses = '*'
max_connections = 200
shared_buffers = 1GB
effective_cache_size = 3GB
maintenance_work_mem = 256MB
checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9
wal_buffers = 16MB
default_statistics_target = 100
random_page_cost = 1.1
effective_io_concurrency = 200
work_mem = 2621kB
huge_pages = off
min_wal_size = 1GB
max_wal_size = 4GB

One small detail that is buried in the PostgreSQL image README (under the “Database Configuration” section) is that if you are using a custom configuration file, we need to add the listen_addresses = '*' value so that other containers can access the database.

traefik:
  options:
    publish:
      - "443:443"
    volume:
      - "/letsencrypt/acme.json:/letsencrypt/acme.json"
  args:
    entryPoints.web.address: ":80"
    entryPoints.websecure.address: ":443"
    entryPoints.web.http.redirections.entryPoint.to: websecure
    entryPoints.web.http.redirections.entryPoint.scheme: https
    entryPoints.web.http.redirections.entrypoint.permanent: true
    certificatesResolvers.letsencrypt.acme.email: "<YOUR_EMAIL_HERE>"
    certificatesResolvers.letsencrypt.acme.storage: "/letsencrypt/acme.json"
    certificatesResolvers.letsencrypt.acme.httpchallenge: true
    certificatesResolvers.letsencrypt.acme.httpchallenge.entrypoint: web

Last, but not least, the necessary configuration of Traefik so that it can generate an SSL certificate with Let’s Encrypt. It mounts the file created in the cloud-init configuration into the Traefik container. This file will store the certificates issued by Let’s Encrypt.

And, believe it or not, that is it! There is much more that we can configure with Kamal but this is the bare minimum I need for now. The only thing remaining is running the setup.

kamal setup

This command will SSH into the servers, install Docker if not installed yet, build your application Docker image, push it to the registry, and start all the containers in both servers. After a couple of minutes (the first run without any cache will take about five minutes) everything is in its place and the web application should be accessible through the browser.

Some useful commands

Kamal provides some useful commands to help us manage the running application and deploy new versions.

kamal deploy

The first one is pretty obvious. Any time I want to deploy a new version of my application, I just need to run this command and that is it! It will create a new Docker image, push it to the registry, and deploy it to the servers through SSH. New deployments usually take less than a minute, not bad!

kamal app logs

This command shows the application logs from all the application servers (even if you have more than one). It has some handy flags:

  • -f or --follow - It follows the logs as they appear.

  • -g <query> or --grep <query> - It searches the logs for the given search parameter.

kamal app exec --interactive --reuse 'bin/rails console'

It is also possible to run shell commands on the running containers (or create temporary containers to run those commands, this is the default behavior). For example, this command runs bin/rails console in the web application container to start an interactive Ruby console. You can run any command you want here.

kamal accessory exec db --interactive --reuse 'psql -U postgres -d postgres'

Another example of running a command in a running container is to open a psql console in the database accessory container. Again, we can put there any shell command and it will run on the given accessory. If you have multiple accessories, you just need to set the correct accessory name.

Why you should do it too

Overall, the process was pretty easy to set up and now I have all the convenience of other platforms on infrastructure that I own. I am not locked in to any particular vendor and I can move things around as I see fit.

Second, this is a good opportunity to learn and exercise different concepts like Terraform, networking, Docker, and Linux in general, … Learning is always a valuable asset to you.

Third, it is surprisingly cheap to run a pretty decent infrastructure that can take you a very long way. The total cost of this (as of May 2024) on Hetzner is just €9.10 per month. For that, you get two Arm64 machines with 2 vCPU, 4 GB of RAM, and 40 GB of storage running Ubuntu 24.04 each. If you don’t need an IPv4 address allocated, you can save €0.50 per server, bringing the total cost to just €8.10 per month. I would bet that for the majority of personal projects out there, and maybe even some early-stage start-ups, this kind of infrastructure is more than enough to last a long time.

Sources

To reach this point some resources were very useful to me. For a Terraform refresher, the official Docker tutorials were very good and straight to the point. To get started with Kamal, their official documentation provided a good starting point. For the Let’s Encrypt setup with Traefik, this blog post from Luiz Kowalski was a great resource.

Creating an inline form on a table with Phoenix LiveView

Originally published on dfilipes.dev. This is the original article; tools and services may have changed since publication.

Contents

  • Step 1 - The movements list table
  • Step 2 - The movement form
  • Step 3 - Adding the form to the movements list table
  • Step 4 - Showing and hiding elements with Phoenix.LiveView.JS
  • Wrapping up

The problem

Recently I was working on a side project that helps me keep track of all my incomes and expenses. When I was looking at the list of movements, I felt the need to be able to quickly edit any entry or add new ones.

The easiest way is to have some sort of button that either moves you to another page or open some modal with the form to create or edit the resource. I thought to myself that would be way cooler if I could do that directly in the same list of movements that I am already looking at.

The solution

The idea is fairly straightforward: in the list of movements, when I click on a row, each field in that row should transform into an editable input. When I submit the form, the list entry returns to the previous state with the updated values. The final product should look like this:

All the code for this can be found in this GitHub repository.

Step 0 - The Phoenix project and the necessary boilerplate

For our example, we will quickly go through the process of setting up an empty project with Phoenix and we will setup Tailwind CSS to help us make it look nicer.

We start by creating a new Phoenix project.

mix phx.new example

With the basic project created, we can generate a simple context for our movements. This Phoenix generator will create for us the Ecto schema and some utility functions.

mix phx.gen.context Accounting Movement movements date:date description:text amount:integer

Our movement schema has three fields:

  • A date when the movement happened;
  • A description to give more context of what the purpose of the movement was;
  • An amount associated with that movement (we could use the money package to better handle this field but for demonstrations purposes having the amount as an integer is good enough).

We can then run the Ecto setup task that will drop the database (if one already exists), creates the database, runs the database migrations and runs the database seeds (that is our case just add some dummy data to our movements table).

mix ecto.reset

Finally, we setup Tailwind CSS so we can use some of its classes to quickly style our application. Tailwind CSS provides setup instructions specific for Phoenix, you can find it here.

Step 1 - The movements list table

We want a simple LiveView that displays a table. We will use some helper classes from Tailwind CSS to style our table.

defmodule ExampleWeb.MovementsListLive do
  use ExampleWeb, :live_view

  alias Example.Accounting

  @impl Phoenix.LiveView
  def mount(_params, _session, socket) do
    socket = assign(socket, :movements, Accounting.list_movements())

    {:ok, socket}
  end

  @impl Phoenix.LiveView
  def render(assigns) do
    ~H"""
    <div class="table w-full text-xs my-4">
      <div class="table-header-group">
        <div class="table-row">
          <div class="table-cell py-2 border-b text-left font-bold w-32">Date</div>
          <div class="table-cell py-2 border-b text-left font-bold">Description</div>
          <div class="table-cell py-2 border-b text-left font-bold w-32">Amount</div>
        </div>
      </div>
      <div class="table-row-group">
        <%= for movement <- @movements do %>
          <div id={"movement-#{movement.id}"} class={"movement movement-#{movement.id} table-row cursor-pointer"}>
            <div class="table-cell py-2 border-y"><%= movement.date %></div>
            <div class="table-cell py-2 border-y"><%= movement.description %></div>
            <div class="table-cell py-2 border-y"><%= movement.amount %></div>
          </div>
        <% end %>
      </div>
    </div>
    """
  end
end

There is nothing special with this LiveView. In the mount/3 function we setup the necessary data to render our page (in this case, a list of all movements in the database is assigned to the socket).

Then, on our render/1 function we have the HEEx template with our table. We have an header with the three fields or our movements (date, description and amount) and then we iterate over the @movements and we set the rows for those movements with the values of those three fields for each one.

With this, we have a functional page that displays the movements in a table. We just need to add the route to our router.ex and we should be able to access it through the browser.

defmodule ExampleWeb.Router do
  use ExampleWeb, :router

  pipeline :browser do
    plug :accepts, ["html"]
    plug :fetch_session
    plug :fetch_live_flash
    plug :put_root_layout, {ExampleWeb.LayoutView, :root}
    plug :protect_from_forgery
    plug :put_secure_browser_headers
  end

  scope "/", ExampleWeb do
    pipe_through :browser

    live "/movements", MovementsListLive, :index
  end

  ...
end

Visiting the /movements page on your browser should display a list of movements.

Step 2 - The movement form

We now want to have a form in the format of a table row that has three inputs, one for each field in own movement. The same form should handle the create and update scenarios for each movement. With that in mind, we can create a LiveComponent for our form with all the logic and markup necessary to render and operate it.

Lets try to look at it bit by bit and go over the detail in each block.

defmodule ExampleWeb.MovementsList.FormComponent do
  use ExampleWeb, :live_component

  alias Example.Accounting
  alias Example.Accounting.Movement

  @impl Phoenix.LiveComponent
  def update(assigns, socket) do
    socket =
      socket
      |> assign(assigns)
      |> assign(:changeset, Accounting.change_movement(assigns.movement))

    {:ok, socket}
  end

  ...
end

First, we define our LiveComponent as FormComponent and we use the update/2 function from the LiveComponent behavior to set some additional assigns. In this case, the only extra assign we want to add is the changeset for the form. Luckily, the Phoenix generator also creates some functions to easily get a changeset with the given movement and params. Since we expect this component to receive a movement from whenever it is used, we get that from the component assigns and use it to set the changeset. In the case of an update operation, we will get the movement we want to change. And in the case of a create operation, we will receive an empty movement. Both cases are covered!

Then, we will have two different events coming in: a validate event to (as the name implies) validate the form, and a save to either create or update the given movement.

@impl Phoenix.LiveComponent
def handle_event("validate", %{"movement" => params}, socket) do
  changeset =
      socket.assigns.movement
      |> Accounting.change_movement(params)
      |> Map.put(:action, :validate)

  socket = assign(socket, :changeset, changeset)
  {:noreply, socket}
end

In the handle_event/3 function for the validate event we just run the received params through the changeset again and assign the resulting changeset on the socket so that it can trigger a new render of the necessary elements on the page. Again, since we are using the movement we have on the socket assigns, both create and update operations are covered.

@impl Phoenix.LiveComponent
def handle_event("save", %{"movement" => params}, socket) do
  case socket.assigns.movement do
    %Movement{id: nil} -> create_movement(socket, params)
    %Movement{} -> update_movement(socket, params)
  end
end

defp create_movement(socket, params) do
  case Accounting.create_movement(params) do
    {:ok, movement} ->
      socket = assign(socket, :changeset, Accounting.change_movement(%Movement{}))
      {:noreply, socket}

    {:error, changeset} ->
      socket = assign(socket, :changeset, changeset)
      {:noreply, socket}
  end
end

defp update_movement(socket, params) do
  case Accounting.update_movement(socket.assigns.movement, params) do
    {:ok, movement} ->
      {:noreply, socket}

    {:error, changeset} ->
      socket = assign(socket, :changeset, changeset)
      {:noreply, socket}
  end
end

In the handle_event/3 function for the save event we start by looking at the movement we have on the socket assigns and decide if we need to create a new movement or update an existing one. Depending on the operation, we use the appropriate functions (also generated by the Phoenix code generator) to either create or update the movement. In case on an error (on any case), we will get a changeset that we can put back on the socket and the form should display any errors found. Another note to the success case of the create operation where we also reset the form so that a new movement can be immediately created after the form is submitted successfully.

@impl Phoenix.LiveComponent
def render(assigns) do
  ~H"""
  <div class="contents">
    <.form let={f} for={@changeset} phx-target={@myself} phx-change="validate" phx-submit="save" as="movement" class="contents">
      <div class={"movement-form #{get_form_class(@movement)}"}>
        <div class="table-cell py-2 pr-1">
          <%= date_input f, :date, class: "rounded w-full text-xs mb-1" %>
          <%= error_tag f, :date, class: "text-xs text-red-500" %>
        </div>
        <div class="table-cell py-2 px-1">
          <%= text_input f, :description, class: "rounded w-full text-xs mb-1" %>
          <%= error_tag f, :description, class: "text-xs text-red-500" %>
        </div>
        <div class="table-cell py-2 pl-1">

        <div class="table-cell pb-2 border-b"></div>

          <button type="submit" class="rounded px-2 py-1 bg-indigo-400 hover:bg-blue-600 text-white">Save</button>

defp get_form_class(%Movement{id: nil}), do: "create-movement-form"
defp get_form_class(%Movement{id: id}), do: "movement-#{id}-form"

And finally, we have the render/1 function with the HEEx template of our form. In practice, there are two new table rows, one with the three different input fields and another one with the submit button. We also use a few Tailwind CSS classes to style the form to make it look nicer.

With that we have a functional form component that we can use on our movements list table.

Step 3 - Adding the form to the movements list table

Back on our MovementsListLive, inside the div with the table-row-group class, we can now use our form component.

@impl Phoenix.LiveView
def render(assigns) do
  ~H"""

And just like that, we have functional forms for each entry on our movements list table!

You might notice that when you save any form, nothing seems to happen. That is because the form submit it being handled on the FormComponent and our movements list is being kept on the MovementsListLive. We need to somehow notify the parent LiveView that it needs to update its records.

LiveComponents have their own state and life-cycle but they run on the parent LiveView process. This means that we can leverage the Elixir process messaging to notify the parent LiveView that it needs to refresh its state. To do that, we can add a send/2 to the success cases of the create and update functions in the FormComponent to send a message to the process stating that that operation occurred.

defp create_movement(socket, params) do
  case Accounting.create_movement(params) do
    {:ok, movement} ->
      socket = assign(socket, :changeset, Accounting.change_movement(%Movement{}))
      send(self(), {:movement_created, movement})
      {:noreply, socket}

    {:error, changeset} ->
      socket = assign(socket, :changeset, changeset)
      {:noreply, socket}
  end
end

defp update_movement(socket, params) do
  case Accounting.update_movement(socket.assigns.movement, params) do
    {:ok, movement} ->
      send(self(), {:movement_updated, movement})
      {:noreply, socket}

    {:error, changeset} ->
      socket = assign(socket, :changeset, changeset)
      {:noreply, socket}
  end
end

On the MovementsListLive we can now handle this incoming messages to update the movements list in the socket state.

@impl Phoenix.LiveView
def handle_info({:movement_created, movement}, socket) do
  socket = assign(socket, :movements, Accounting.list_movements())

  {:noreply, socket}
end

@impl Phoenix.LiveView
def handle_info({:movement_updated, movement}, socket) do
  movements = 
    Enum.map(
      socket.assigns.movements, 
      &if(&1.id == movement.id, do: movement, else: &1)
    )

  socket = assign(socket, :movements, movements)

  {:noreply, socket}
end

Now if you try to submit any of the forms in the page, the changes are now done automatically after the successful form submit. We now have functional forms but the objective is to only show them if we click on a row in the movements list table.

We could send events through the wire from the browser to server to control if a form show be shown or not and that would trigger a new render of the LiveView. But that seems overkill for just showing and hiding elements on the browser. Luckily, there is a better way!

Step 4 - Showing and hiding elements with Phoenix.LiveView.JS

With the Phoenix.LiveView.JS utilities we can do some common client-side operations like adding and removing classes to elements, setting attributes, dispatch DOM events and even apply transitions to elements.

Lets start by making the form elements hidden by default with the help of the helper class hidden from Tailwind CSS. This class is just a shortcut to set the display: none; on the element.

@impl Phoenix.LiveComponent
def render(assigns) do
  ~H"""
  <div class="contents">
    <.form let={f} for={@changeset} phx-target={@myself} phx-change="validate" phx-submit="save" as="movement" class="contents">
      <div class={"movement-form #{get_form_class(@movement)} hidden"}>
        ...
      </div>
      <div class={"movement-form #{get_form_class(@movement)} hidden"}>
        ...
      </div>
    </.form>
  </div>
  """
end

With our form elements hidden, we should just see the movements list table like we have in the beginning. Now we need to show the form when there is a click on a table row. In here, we set a few requirements:

  • Only one form should be visible at a time;
  • If there is already a visible form, when clicking on another table row, we should hide the previous form;
  • Same thing applies if the create movement form is also visible;
  • When displaying a form, we should automatically hide the movement table row that was clicked.

Having this in mind, we can use the Phoenix.LiveView.JS utilities to create a show_form/2 function on the MovementsListLive that does exactly this.

defp show_form(js \\ %JS{}, movement)

defp show_form(js, %Movement{id: nil}) do
  js
  |> JS.hide(to: ".movement-form")                  # Hide any visible form
  |> JS.show(to: ".movement", display: "table-row") # Display any previously hidden table row
  |> JS.show(                                       # Display create movement form
    to: ".create-movement-form",
    display: "table-row",
    transition: {"ease-in duration-150", "opacity-0", "opacity-100"},
    time: 150
  )
end

defp show_form(js, movement) do
  js
  |> JS.hide(to: ".movement-form")                  # Hide any visible form
  |> JS.show(to: ".movement", display: "table-row") # Display any previously hidden table row
  |> JS.hide(to: ".movement-#{movement.id}")        # Hide clicked table row
  |> JS.show(                                       # Display update movement form
    to: ".movement-#{movement.id}-form",
    display: "table-row",
    transition: {"ease-in duration-150", "opacity-0", "opacity-100"},
    time: 150
  )
end

Here we have a show_form/2 and with it we can hide and show elements in the page thanks to the appropriate CSS classes. We even set some transitions to make it look a little bit nicer when the form element is getting shown on the page. Now we can use this function on our render/1 to display the forms when clicked. To do that, we can add the function call to a phx-click binding on the element we want. Instead of passing a string with the event name on phx-click binding, instead we use a function call to our show_form/2 function.

@impl Phoenix.LiveView
def render(assigns) do
  ~H"""
  <div class="my-4">
    <button type="button"
            phx-click={show_form(%Movement{})}
            class="rounded px-3 py-2 bg-indigo-400 hover:bg-blue-600 text-white text-sm">

  <div class="table w-full text-xs my-4">

        <.live_component module={ExampleWeb.MovementsList.FormComponent}

Now we already have a way of displaying the create and update forms but we should also have a way to dismiss them without submitting the form. We can do that with the same strategy we used to display the forms in the first place. Lets start by creating a hide_form/2 function on the MovementsListLive.

defp hide_form(js \\ %JS{}, movement)

And now we have a function “Cancel” button that dismisses the form correctly.

There is just one small detail left to complete our feature. When submitting the form, we should dismiss it as well. The question here is, how can we trigger our Phoenix.LiveView.JS changes from the server?

In this Fly.io blog post we are presented with a cool trick for this. Basically, we can push an event from the server to the client and in the client we can look at the event message, get some element from the DOM, look for a specific data attribute with our Phoenix.LiveView.JS changes and apply them.

Going back to our render/1 function on the MovementsListLive, lets add the data-hide-form attribute with the Phoenix.LiveView.JS structure to hide a form.

@impl Phoenix.LiveView
def render(assigns) do
  ~H"""
  <div class="my-4">
    ...
  </div>
  <div class="table w-full text-xs my-4">
    <div class="table-header-group">
      ...
    </div>
    <div class="table-row-group">
      ...
      <%= for movement <- @movements do %>
        <div id={"movement-#{movement.id}"}
             class={"movement movement-#{movement.id} table-row cursor-pointer"}
             phx-click={show_form(movement)}
             data-hide-form={hide_form(@movement)}>
          ...
        </div>
        ...
      <% end %>
    </div>
  </div>
  """
end

And in the handle_info/2 functions for the notification messages from the form, lets push an event to the client to inform him of the change.

@impl Phoenix.LiveView
def handle_info({:movement_created, movement}, socket) do
  socket =
    socket
    ...
    |> push_event("js-exec", %{
      to: ".movement-#{movement.id}",
      attr: "data-hide-form"
    })

  {:noreply, socket}
end

@impl Phoenix.LiveView
def handle_info({:movement_updated, movement}, socket) do
  ...

  socket =
    socket
    ...
    |> push_event("js-exec", %{
      to: ".movement-#{movement.id}",
      attr: "data-hide-form"
    })

  {:noreply, socket}
end

We are sending an event name js-exec with a payload that contains the element we want to target (that has the data-hide-form attribute) and the attribute name itself.

The final step is just add the listener for this event on the client script to handle the event and apply the Phoenix.LiveView.JS changes. On our assets/js/app.js we can add the following:

window.addEventListener("phx:js-exec", ({ detail }) => {
    document.querySelectorAll(detail.to).forEach(el => {
        liveSocket.execJS(el, el.getAttribute(detail.attr))
    })
})

And that is it! Our forms should now be shown or hidden correctly the way that we wanted.

Wrapping up

In a fairly simple use case we could see in action several parts of Phoenix.LiveView and how they interact. We could also experiment with Phoenix.LiveView.JS that can replace Alpine.js for client side interactions.
